title: Software Vulnerabilities and Attacks
objective: Study-guide review — CISSP — Domain 8: Software Development Security: Software Vulnerabilities and Attacks.

items: Occurs when a program writes data beyond the boundaries of allocated memory (buffer)
Attacker overwrites adjacent memory, potentially including the instruction pointer (return address)
Once the instruction pointer is overwritten, whatever code has been placed in the buffer can be executed, all under the security context of the application
Stack-based buffer overflow — overflows the call stack; most common type
Heap-based buffer overflow — overflows dynamically allocated memory on the heap
Defenses: bounds checking, safe string functions, stack canaries, ASLR (Address Space Layout Randomization), DEP/NX (Data Execution Prevention / No-Execute), using memory-safe languages

blocks.text: Buffer overflows are one of the most dangerous and well-understood software vulnerabilities. The attack works by providing more input than the buffer can hold, causing the excess data to overwrite adjacent memory. If the attacker carefully crafts the overflow data, they can overwrite the return address (instruction pointer) on the stack to point to their malicious code (shellcode). The key principle: the malicious code executes with the same privileges as the vulnerable application. If the application runs as root/administrator, the attacker gains full system control. Modern defenses make exploitation more difficult but do not eliminate the vulnerability:

items: ASLR — randomizes memory addresses so attackers cannot predict where their shellcode will be loaded
DEP/NX — marks memory regions as non-executable, preventing code execution in data areas
Stack canaries — special values placed between buffers and control data; if overwritten, the application terminates before the malicious code can execute
Memory-safe languages (Java, Python, Rust) — prevent buffer overflows through bounds checking

blocks.title: Exam trap
blocks.text: ⚠️ Exam Trap: Buffer overflow executes code in the security context of the vulnerable application. This is why running services with least privilege is critical — even if a buffer overflow is exploited, the damage is limited to the application's privileges.

items: SQL Injection — inserting malicious SQL commands into input fields that are used in database queries
Defense: parameterized queries (prepared statements), stored procedures, input validation
Command Injection (OS Injection) — inserting operating system commands through application input
Defense: avoid calling OS commands from application code; if necessary, use strict allowlisting
LDAP Injection — inserting malicious LDAP statements into queries
XML Injection / XXE (XML External Entity) — exploiting XML parsers to read files, perform SSRF, or cause DoS
NoSQL Injection — similar to SQL injection but targeting NoSQL databases

blocks.text: Injection attacks consistently rank among the most critical web application vulnerabilities. The root cause is always the same: the application fails to properly separate code from data, allowing attacker-supplied data to be interpreted as commands. SQL injection example:

items: Vulnerable code: SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = '" + userInput + "'"
Malicious input: ' OR '1'='1
Resulting query: SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = '' OR '1'='1' — returns all users

blocks.text: The parameterized query defense works because the database engine treats the parameter as a data value, not part of the SQL command, regardless of what the user provides:

items: Safe code: SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = ? (with parameter binding)
Attacker injects malicious scripts (usually JavaScript) into web pages viewed by other users
Reflected (non-persistent) XSS — malicious script is reflected off a web server (e.g., in error messages, search results); victim must click a crafted link
Stored (persistent) XSS — malicious script is permanently stored on the server (e.g., in a forum post, comment, database record); affects all users who view the content
DOM-based XSS — vulnerability exists in client-side JavaScript that manipulates the DOM without proper sanitization
Consequences: session hijacking, credential theft, defacement, malware distribution, keylogging
Defenses: output encoding, input validation, Content Security Policy (CSP), HttpOnly cookie flag

blocks.text: The nonpersistent (reflected) cross-site scripting vulnerability requires the victim to click a specially crafted link containing the malicious script. The script is sent to the server, which "reflects" it back in the response. The victim's browser then executes the script in the context of the vulnerable website. Stored XSS is more dangerous because it does not require victim interaction beyond visiting the page — the malicious script is stored on the server and delivered to every user who views the affected page. Frameworks that automatically implement anti-XSS protections (automatic output encoding) significantly reduce XSS risk. Content Security Policy (CSP) headers provide an additional layer of defense by instructing browsers to only execute scripts from approved sources. ⚠️ Exam Trap: Reflected XSS = requires victim to click a link (non-persistent). Stored XSS = stored on the server, affects all viewers (persistent). Stored is more dangerous because it doesn't require user interaction beyond normal browsing.

items: Attacker tricks a victim's browser into making unintended requests to a vulnerable web application where the victim is authenticated
Exploits the browser's automatic inclusion of cookies/credentials with requests
Example: victim is logged into their bank; visits a malicious page that contains a hidden form submitting a transfer request to the bank
Defenses: CSRF tokens (unique, unpredictable tokens per session/request), SameSite cookie attribute, re-authentication for sensitive operations, checking Referer/Origin headers
Race condition — occurs when the outcome depends on the timing or sequence of events, and multiple processes/threads compete for shared resources
TOCTOU (Time-of-Check to Time-of-Use) — specific race condition where a resource's state changes between the time it is checked and the time it is used
Example: checking file permissions (time-of-check), then opening the file (time-of-use) — an attacker may change the file between check and use
Defenses: atomic operations, proper locking mechanisms, minimizing the window between check and use, avoiding shared state

blocks.text: TOCTOU vulnerabilities are particularly insidious because they exploit the inherent gap between verifying a condition and acting on it. In a multithreaded or multi-user environment, another process can modify the resource in that gap. Common TOCTOU scenarios:

items: File access: check if user has permission to read file → attacker replaces file with a symbolic link to a sensitive file → application reads the sensitive file
Authentication: verify user's access level → user's access is revoked → application performs the privileged action with stale authorization

blocks.title: Exam trap
blocks.text: ⚠️ Exam Trap: TOCTOU is a specific type of race condition. If the exam mentions "time-of-check to time-of-use" or describes a scenario where a resource changes between verification and use, the answer is TOCTOU.

items: Vertical escalation — gaining higher privileges than authorized (e.g., regular user → administrator)
Horizontal escalation — accessing resources of another user at the same privilege level (e.g., accessing another user's account)
Attack vectors: exploiting vulnerabilities (buffer overflow), misconfigurations, social engineering, credential theft
Defenses: least privilege, proper access controls, patching, monitoring for anomalous access patterns
Backdoor — undocumented access method intentionally or unintentionally left in software
Trapdoor — essentially the same as a backdoor; sometimes used to describe a developer's maintenance access point
May be installed by: malware, attackers who have gained access, or developers during development (should be removed before release)
Defenses: code review, integrity monitoring, behavior analysis, following secure SDLC practices
